name: Cannikin
problem: Serving many LoRA services that share one base LLM while each service has its own SLO; SLO-oblivious multi-LoRA serving causes large SLO violations for some services.
mechanism: Optimizes the minimum SLO attainment across services (the lagger service) with an SLO-aware scheduler using efficient deadline estimation; detects interference between services and removes its bias; design motivated by a workload analysis of a real-world trace (all per abstract).
workload: Abstract says a workload analysis of a real-world trace motivates the design; trace source, adapter-popularity distribution and any Zipf parameter NOT verified (full text paywalled). The paper cites ShareGPT as a dataset (reference 34 of the Crossref list).
headline: Up to 3.6x higher request rate or 2.8x more burstiness while keeping SLO attainment above 90% (baseline not named in the abstract).
code_note: not found (no arXiv version; author homepage horsebridge.github.io links only the IEEE PDF; Crossref/OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar records show no code link; web search found none)
evidence: OpenAlex abstract summary; Crossref metadata and 55-entry reference list; Semantic Scholar record (abstract elided by publisher); author homepage; citing text in InfiniLoRA arXiv html (describes Cannikin as request scheduling plus adapter-aware cache management and as optimizing SLO attainment for the worst-served adapter service). IEEE Xplore and computer.org pages returned no content; the IEEE staging PDF fetch was denied by the permission classifier and not retried.

name: Rock
problem: Serving thousands of LoRA adapters for cloud image-generation (diffusion) under bursty traffic (up to 90x normal rate), heterogeneous task types and costly adapter management.
mechanism: Three-layer design (physical GPU grouping, logical partitions, GPU adapter cache): tasks clustered into queues with Gaussian Mixture Models and matched to GPUs by a weighted bipartite graph (Top-K, K=3, refreshed every 90 s); adapter replicas follow popularity; LRU eviction at 85% partition memory.
num_adapters: 200+ adapters associated with requests in the evaluation (title says thousands)
workload: Preprocessed three-month production data (prompts, task types, 20-50 iterations, 512^2-1024^2 resolutions); long-tailed popularity: about 20% of adapters serve about 80% of requests (Fig. 9) while the introduction says top 5% serve over 60% (inconsistent). Related paper 2609.23321 says Rock characterizes the public GenTD26 trace (24 days, Nov-Dec 2024), which conflicts with the three-month claim; unresolved.
baselines: Proactive (prediction and preloading adapted from LLM serving)
hardware: 64 GPUs on 16 nodes: A100, A40, V100, RTX 3090 (128 CPU cores, 1 TB RAM, 100 Gbps RDMA per node); CUDA 12.2
headline: Average latency -25.4%, -26.1%, -16.6% vs RROD, LRUMS, Proactive (abstract: 16-26%); P99 under 80 s vs about 100 s; cache hit rate 84.1%; adapter updates -77% vs RROD and -44% vs Proactive.
built_on: PEFT (HF) extended with adapter management plus Kubernetes scheduler hooks; PyTorch/Diffusers
code_note: none in paper; web search found none
evidence: Author-hosted PDF (yanyinglin.github.io/assets/pdf/Cluster25.pdf) read through the fetch tool summarizer, full text; Crossref metadata; web search for code

name: Dop (Dynamic Operator Optimization)
problem: Multi-tenant LoRA serving leaves GPUs underused because the batched cross-adapter operator (Punica SGMV) is not tuned to each batch scenario.
mechanism: Auto-tunes the SGMV operator per scenario: a Search Space Constructor builds a hierarchical space (high-level structure vs low-level implementation) and an evolutionary-search Optimization Engine guided by a performance cost model refines implementations (300 mutation iterations per scenario, about 1.5 h total).
num_adapters: not stated (workloads defined relative to request count n)
ranks: 16 in microbenchmark; end-to-end rank not stated
workload: Distinct (one adapter per request), Uniform (ceil(sqrt n) adapters), Skewed (Zipf alpha=1.5), Identical; throughput test 1,000 requests (~101k tokens), max batch 32, FCFS, single A100; model-switch cost excluded.
baseline_versions: PyTorch 2.1.2, CUDA 12.4; non-Punica baselines load LoRA via PEFT; no baseline release versions
hardware: NVIDIA A100 40GB; RTX 3090 (Llama-2 only on A100)
headline: 1.30-1.46x throughput over Punica (Skewed, 7B: about 1,460 vs 1,044 tokens/s); operator latency -56.21% (RTX 3090, batch 31, Distinct) and -54.03% (A100, batch 45, Skewed).
code_note: none in paper text; not searched beyond the paper and listing pages
evidence: AAAI PDF (ojs.aaai.org download link) read through the fetch tool summarizer; Semantic Scholar and mlanthology records for authors/abstract. exact flag inferred (operator tuning), not stated.

name: LayerLoom
venue: arXiv preprint 2026 (v1, 31 Oct 2026, cs.LG; ICML-style template; no venue stated). Supersedes the low-confidence stub num 81 in all.json.
problem: Co-serving LoRA fine-tuning and inference on the same GPUs: per-iteration backward budgets make fine-tuning dictate inference latency during bursts.
mechanism: Schedules LoRA backward work at layer (not iteration) granularity: same-layer backward tasks ride the inference forward pass, admitted per layer up to the latency slack of in-flight requests; a wavefront of staggered fine-tuning microbatches with scheduler-guided host-memory offloading; a fused kernel reads each base-weight tile once for paired forward and backward GEMMs.
quality_cost: Same losses as FlexLLM without inference load (20 updates, 1,280 samples); under load losses deviate from FlexLLM by the same order as two FlexLLM runs deviate from each other
workload: Inference arrivals from BurstGPT (public) segments of 4K requests chosen at 10th/50th/90th percentile of arrival burstiness, prompt/decode lengths from ShareGPT; evaluation replays the high-burstiness trace at Mid and High loads (calibrated so inference alone attains 100% and 98% joint SLO); fine-tuning samples from Sky-T1 (up to 8K tokens), 128-token microbatches. The abstract phrase production trace refers to BurstGPT.
baseline_versions: FlexLLM (Oliaro et al., 2026) on FlexFlow Serve and Legion; no release version; all systems run cuBLAS kernels without Legion tracing
metrics: joint SLO attainment (TTFT<=5 s and TPOT<=168 ms)
headline: Joint SLO attainment +21.8 points (Mid: 94.4% vs 72.6%) and +13.5 points (High: 88.8% vs 75.2%) over FlexLLM with fine-tuning throughput comparable or up to 12% higher; P99 TTFT 55.4 s to 14.2 s (Mid); shared-weight down_proj kernel up to 1.58x.
built_on: FlexLLM / FlexFlow Serve / Legion (2.9K lines C++/CUDA added)

name: AuLoRA
problem: Multi-tenant LoRA serving loads adapters from host memory on demand and batches work, creating loading/computation dependencies that inflate TTFT.
mechanism: Layer-wise-priority adapter loading overlapped with backbone computation; intra-layer pipelined load/compute; dynamic batching that searches a batching plan accounting for kernel launch overhead.
headline: Up to 3.03x lower TTFT and 1.27x higher throughput vs S-LoRA.

name: MixLoRA (ICPP 2025 serving framework)
venue: ACM ICPP 2025 (DOI 10.1145/3754598.3754605; published online 2025-12-20). NOT the arXiv 2404.15159 MixLoRA mixture-of-experts fine-tuning paper.
problem: Existing multi-LoRA inference systems such as Punica under-utilize the GPU and lose throughput when concurrent requests use adapters of different ranks.
mechanism: CUDA-stream based multi-worker framework: a scheduler picks the number of concurrent workers from model size, request characteristics and device information; each worker serves requests of a single fixed rank, avoiding rank-aligned batching.
headline: Up to 1.2x higher throughput than state-of-the-art solutions.

name: CoLoRA
problem: Multi-tenant LoRA serving has conflicting QoS goals (online latency vs offline throughput), high adapter loading and switching costs and static batching that fits dynamic load poorly.
mechanism: Unified scheduler: Adaptive Priority Scheduling (priority from queueing delay, adapter residency, SLA urgency); Adapter-Aware Scheduling (eviction score from recency, SLA urgency, predicted hotness, tenant fairness; prefers GPUs with the adapter resident); Load-Aware Batch Scheduling (batch size from load, grouping by adapter).
headline: Up to 55% higher throughput, up to 34% lower P95 latency, GPU utilization up to 86.3%, cache hit rate up to +42%, Jain fairness up to 0.95 (relative to unnamed baselines).
code_note: not found; slides give no link
evidence: ASP-DAC 2026 slide PDF (aspdac.com archive 4A-1.pdf) read through the fetch tool; base model, adapter count and ranks not given on the slides

name: UniLoRA
venue: IEEE ICASSP 2026 (pp 20516-20520; DOI 10.1109/icassp55912.2026.11462889; venue inferred from DOI prefix)
problem: LoRA management in multi-tenant LLM services suffers slow dynamic loading, weak isolation, poor GPU utilization and cross-framework incompatibility.
mechanism: SLA-aware scheduler (DQN policy, asynchronous loading, sandbox isolation); adaptive memory management (predictive caching, LoRA-aware CUDA kernels, adaptive batching); standardized JSON adapter protocol with conversion toolchain.
headline: 1.8x faster P99 latency, SLA compliance above 92%, 90% of unauthorized adapters blocked, 1.6x faster adapter conversion (baselines not named in the abstract summary).

name: LoRA-PIM
problem: Adapter swapping from host to GPU memory costs 8-20 ms and energy in multi-adapter serving.
mechanism: Processing-in-memory DRAM architecture that applies quantized LoRA delta weights to base weights in place using an 8-bit masked XOR/ADD unit per sense-amplifier slice.
headline: Adapter-switch latency 9.6 ms (GPU+S-LoRA) to 50 microseconds (99.5% lower) and 70% lower per-token energy in simulation, 2% bank-area overhead, accuracy preserved.

name: CLIMB
problem: When the active adapter working set exceeds the K device slots left after the KV cache, non-resident adapters stall shared execution and TTFT tail latency collapses (residency cliff).
mechanism: Minimal ingress controller: feasibility-first admission, queues non-resident adapters outside the engine, prioritizes VIP traffic and rotates background adapters round-robin.
headline: At matched throughput (10.66 rps) VIP TTFT p99 from 38.7 s to 13.1 s on a cliff-inducing workload; VIP engine latency about 0.13 s; no throughput loss in evaluated settings.

name: DyMerge-LoRA

headline: Up to 1.1-4x higher inference throughput than state-of-the-art methods, lower TTFT and lower GPU memory (baselines not named in the abstract).

name: LoRATEE
problem: Multi-tenant LoRA deployments expose model parameters and data to malicious servers.
mechanism: Runs LoRA adapters inside a server-side TEE with one-time-pad encryption for data transfer, dynamic adapter prefetching to cut I/O latency, and a PEFT-based adapter-module equivalence-sharing strategy to optimize loading.
headline: Abstract states inference efficiency is maintained while securing multi-tenant LoRA LLMs; no numbers, models, baselines or hardware in the abstract.

name: FlashServe
venue: Preprints.org 2025 (doi 10.20944/preprints202512.1908.v1, posted 22 Dec 2025; not peer reviewed)
problem: Serverless LLM serving has slow, costly cold starts from loading multi-GB weights; includes sharing a base across many fine-tuned variants.
mechanism: Tiered memory snapshotting (host DRAM staging, PCIe DMA to GPU); hybrid Prophet-LSTM forecasting to pre-warm pods; LoRA adapter multiplexing (50+ adapters on one base instance).
workload: Azure Functions trace for cold-start/autoscaling; LoRA part uses synthetic adapters with no named trace.
hardware: 8 servers x 8 A100-80GB, PCIe Gen4, 512 GB DDR4, 2x2TB NVMe, 100 Gbps InfiniBand; CUDA 12.1, PyTorch 2.1
headline: Cold start up to 49x vs S3 loading and 3.3x vs ServerlessLLM; 32% lower GPU idle cost; TTFT under 1 s for 95% of requests; LoRA multiplexing Table 3: 128 adapters in 18.2 GB at 76 req/s with 2.1 ms swap vs S-LoRA 32 adapters 15.2 GB, 78 req/s, 12.5 ms (text claims 4% degradation, table implies about 7%; swap stated as under 2 or 2.5 ms in text vs 1.8/2.1 in table).
built_on: custom (about 12,000 lines Python and C++); vLLM baseline

name: BitDelta
venue: arXiv v3 (13 Oct 2024); venue not stated in fetched text
problem: Serving or storing many full-parameter fine-tunes of one base model is costly in GPU memory, storage and load time.
mechanism: Quantizes each fine-tune delta to 1 bit (sign mask plus one learned scale per matrix, scale distillation on 800 C4 samples) so one high-precision base plus many 1-bit deltas can be served; batched decoding uses a BitBLAS W_INT1 A_FP16 kernel.
quality_cost: Abstract: without compromising performance; evaluated on MT-Bench, ARC, BBH, HellaSwag, TruthfulQA, LAMBADA, Winogrande, GSM8K (per-benchmark numbers not extracted)
num_adapters: batch of distinct fine-tuned models B (latency sweep up to B beyond 16; exact maximum not extracted)
ranks: n/a (full-parameter deltas; S-LoRA comparison at rank memory-matched to 1-bit delta)
workload: Latency microbenchmarks: each model receives one distinct request simultaneously, input length 128, decoding only; no arrival trace.
hardware: A100 80GB (500 W limit); compression on 1x and 6x A100
headline: More than 10x GPU memory reduction and more than 10x lower per-user decoding latency than the naive method in the B>=16 regime (Llama 2-7B, A100).
code_note: link given in paper; repo not opened
evidence: arxiv.org/html/2402.10193 (v3) sections 3-4 read via curl; math annotations recovered from raw html

name: Per-Axis Weight Deltas
venue: Workshop paper (CCFM: AI That Keeps Up, Workshop on Continual and Compatible Foundation Model Updates); parent conference not stated
problem: Serving many task-specialized LLM variants is limited by large checkpoints and cold-start latency.
mechanism: 1-bit sign delta with per-row/column FP16 scale vectors learned on 150 C4 samples; loader transfers packed deltas in one operation per module; no dense reconstruction.
quality_cost: Avg zero-shot accuracy 70.23 vs 69.95 (BitDelta scalar) vs 69.26 (uncompressed) on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; Qwen3-14B 71.71 vs 71.05 vs 71.34; Phi-4-reasoning 71.00 vs 71.06 vs 70.74
num_adapters: 1 delta per pair evaluated (no multi-tenant serving experiment; stated as future work)
workload: No request workload; cold-start load-time measurement averaged over 10 runs.
headline: Llama-3.1-8B delta artifact about 2.97 GB, 5.24x smaller than FP16 checkpoint; applying the delta loads in 0.80 s vs 2.08 s for the full FP16 checkpoint.
code_note: link given in abstract; repo not opened

name: Delta-CoMe
venue: arXiv (venue not stated in fetched text)
problem: Multi-tenant serving of several task-specific fine-tunes; low-rank or low-bit delta compression hurts task-specific models (math, code, chat, multimodal).
mechanism: Mixed-precision delta quantization: SVD of the delta, higher-bit representation for singular vectors with large singular values, lower bits for the long tail; Triton kernel.
quality_cost: Performs comparably to full fine-tuned models and beats low-rank and BitDelta baselines (WizardMath, MagicoderS, WizardCoder, Llama-2-chat, LLaVA-1.5 pairs)
num_adapters: up to 50 deltas loaded on one 80 GB GPU (Llama-2-7B deltas)
workload: No request workload; memory table and kernel latency vs batch size/hidden size only.
headline: More than 10x GPU memory and disk saving; 50 models fit on one 80 GB GPU where the uncompressed setting is OOM at 8 models; Triton kernel about 3x faster than the PyTorch implementation.
code_note: paper says code will be publicly available at this link; repo not opened

name: ME-Switch
venue: arXiv v2 (26 Oct 2024); venue not stated in fetched text
problem: Serving multiple fine-tuned expert LLMs: loading all experts is impractical and switching incurs I/O cost; the appropriate expert for a request is not known in advance.
mechanism: Salient-aware mixed-precision delta compression (salient input channels kept FP16, rest about 2 bits) with a Triton fused dequantization-GEMM kernel enabling model-level batching, plus a model-level router doing domain classification (DistilBERT or small LLM).
quality_cost: Near lossless on MMLU, GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval, MBPP for three Mistral-7B experts
num_adapters: 16 Mistral-7B experts on one A100 (naive OOM)
workload: Decoding latency vs number of models, input length 128; no arrival trace.
hardware: NVIDIA A100 80GB (compression on 2-4 A100; router on 8 A100)
headline: Model size reduced 1.74x for three Mistral-7B experts (up to 3.63x for the LLaMA-13B family); lower latency than naive once more than 4 models are served; 16 models served on a single A100.

name: LoRA Land / LoRAX evaluation (Predibase technical report)
problem: Assessing whether many LoRA fine-tuned LLMs can be served on one GPU in production and how much adapter switching costs.
mechanism: Evaluates the existing LoRAX server (dynamic adapter loading, continuous multi-adapter batching, tiered weight caching) rather than proposing a new mechanism; also reports a 310-model fine-tuning quality study.
workload: Random payloads of 30-500 input and 1-120 output tokens, 1-50 concurrent users, requests spread randomly over 25 adapter endpoints; 2-minute runs; not a trace.
headline: 25 adapters and 100 concurrent users add 7.21 ms average total request time vs base (199.02 vs 191.81 ms); no significant TTFT or throughput difference between base and 25 adapters up to 50 concurrent users; TTFT about 200 ms or lower.

name: MoLoRA (per-token adapter routing)
venue: arXiv 2026 (v1, 16 Mar 2026); an ICML 2026 poster listing appeared in search results but was not opened
problem: Multi-adapter serving routes whole sequences to one adapter, forcing K passes for K-modality or mixed-capability requests.
mechanism: Per-token routing (vocabulary-based for multimodal, learned gating for semantic domains) so one pass serves all adapters; static hot-set adapter memory enabling CUDA-graph capture; Triton tensor-core grouped kernel with adaptive tiling.
quality_cost: Qwen3-1.7B with MoLoRA exceeds Qwen3-8B on GSM8K (+14%), MATH (+8%), BBH (+2.5%), GPQA (+2.1%); the router is learned (quality effect of routing, not of serving)
num_adapters: 4 (4 modalities; Qwen3-4B with 4 rank-8 adapters); adapter-count sweep 4-64 in layout microbenchmark
workload: Synthetic token/modality mixes (uniform 25% each, skewed 80/10/5/5, extreme 95/2/2/1), no request arrival process; median of 1000 iterations.
headline: K=4 modalities: 5.88 ms to 1.43 ms (4.1x) from pass reduction, 5.5x with hot-set and CUDA graphs vs per-sequence+paging (7.48 ms); Qwen3-4B 4.1-4.3x with diverse adapters, 1.0x with a single adapter; kernel 1.3-2.7x over S-LoRA BGMV at batch 256-2048.

name: Adapter co-occurrence characterization (GenTD26)
problem: Production LoRA adapter co-occurrence, popularity and latency impact in a diffusion inference service were not systematically characterized; informs caching, preloading and GPU memory management.
mechanism: Graph-theoretic characterization of an adapter co-occurrence network from Alibaba GenTD26 plus a top-k co-occurrence preloading strategy evaluated offline.
base_models: 86 base models in the request trace (diffusion)
num_adapters: 874 unique LoRA adapters (26,823 requests, 24 days, 143 containers)
workload: Alibaba commercial image-generation service trace GenTD26 (15 Nov to 8 Dec 2024); 77.7% of requests carry no adapter, 20.7% one, 1.6% several; adapter popularity heavy-tailed: rank-frequency slope alpha=1.30 (descriptive), top 5% of adapters 53.5% of occurrences, Gini 0.749; MLE power-law fit alpha=1.56 rejected (p=0.003). Request trace has no adapter ids and processing trace has no timestamps, so they cannot be linked.
headline: First adapter adds 66.1% execution latency (39.2 s vs 23.6 s); preloading on top-k co-occurrence covers 81.0% of test co-occurrence pairs at k=3 (offline).
code_note: none stated in the sections read
evidence: arxiv.org/html/2609.23321 abstract, sections 1, 4, 8 read via curl. Public availability of GenTD26 not confirmed in text read. IN is borderline: characterization paper.
